evidence.title: Adding agents yields task-dependent gains and losses
evidence.observation: Source-reported finding: Controlled agent-system comparisons report both collaboration benefits and performance losses depending on task structure, models and coordination overhead. Some decomposable tasks improve; additional agents do not uniformly improve performance. Observation period and measurement context: Experiment calendar dates not established.
evidence.evidence_standing: Source-reported bounded account; study or measurement; not independently reproduced
evidence.glossary_fit: Illustrative or qualifying; does not validate a definition

source_locations.SRC-127: Preprint; author summary; repository changelog; architecture_selection_eval.py protocol docstring

evidence.limitations: Designed architectures rather than spontaneous coordination. v1 had 180 configurations/four benchmarks; v3 has 260/six. Author repository v2.2.3 corrects selection of 270 versus 260 configurations. Scripts were not executed; full journal article was inaccessible. No generalized architecture-selection accuracy is asserted here.
evidence.open_questions: Transfer to other populations, tasks and operating environments remains unestablished. Missing measurement details are not inferred.
evidence.support_assessment: Commons interpretation: Qualifies a universal scaling-benefit assumption. Prediction estimates depend on holdout unit and measured coordination features, so they are excluded from this observation.
evidence.dispute_status: See source version and dispute qualifications; no systematic clearance claimed.
evidence.verification_status: Not independently verified by the Commons

terms.name: Cross-system feedback
terms.definition: A pattern in which an action or output from one technical or organizational process affects activity elsewhere and subsequent responses modify conditions for additional participants. Many response paths may exist; there need not be a single linear loop.

relationships.explanation: Qualifies assumptions that interaction among more agents necessarily improves system results; does not itself demonstrate spontaneous feedback.
